newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Moody's report disappoints Hungary - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Moody's report disappoints Hungary - analysts.

text.p: A Moody's Investors Services report which praised Hungary's progress in economic reform but stopped short of upgrading its debt was a disappointment for Hungary, analysts said on Friday.
"It's certainly a cold shower for the National Bank of Hungary (NBH)," said Istvan Racz, an analyst for Credit Suisse-First Boston in Budapest.

"It's basically a report which is praising the performance of the Hungarian government and the National Bank...but on the other hand the agency seems to have reservations -- the same ones it had earlier -- that debts and deficits are high and inflation is quite questionable," Racz said.

The NBH had no official comment on the Moody's report, released on Thursday. Moody's retained a Ba1 rating for foreign currency debt and Ba2 for bank deposits, saying these put Hungary "at the top of the speculative grade ladder".
It said the ratings "reflect the progress the country has made in its economic reform, but also reflect the fact that more needs to be done".

Suzanne Hallergard, an ING Barings economist based in London, said she thought Moody's had issued its comment to quell speculation after smaller ratings agencies, among them Thomson BankWatch, Duff & Phelps and IBCA, earlier this year improved Hungary's credit rating to investment grade.
"I think there was a lot of speculation on the market," Hallergard said.

"It was our view that both Moody's and Standard & Poor's were focusing very much on debt ratios and on the budget performance and wanted to make sure that the tax reforms and social security reforms that are presently in Parliament will go through before they move on an upgrade," she said.
Hallergard added that if Parliament passed the necessary legislation as expected this year, upgrades might come in the first or second quarter of next year.
Racz said, however, that the government's commitment to the reforms was beyond serious doubt, and suggested that the big ratings agencies were a bit slow off the mark.
"The actual credit performance of the National Bank is now beyond doubt better than what would be suggested on the basis of the existing credit ratings from Moody's and S&P's," he said.
"It seems that these two agencies are now lagging a little bit behind the market's current evaluations."
